sections.title: What Orbit does
sections.html: Orbit keeps track of the things a home has to remember: servicing, renewals, inspections, contracts and cover, and who in the household shares them. It runs on your own server. The website tells the story; this page is the plain description behind it. The v1 charter is the formal statement of what a stable release must do.

sections.title: The screens
sections.html:
#The screens

The screenshots below are the real app, filled with made-up data for a made-up household. They hold no real accounts or settings.

#Your sky

The home screen is "your sky": the year drawn as a dial, with your household at the centre and today at the top. Each thing you look after is a body on its own orbit. The closer it sits to the centre, the sooner it is due; overdue items sit inside the event horizon, the dashed red ring around your sun. The "key" tab on the right explains the colours and sizes. The search box at the bottom, "explore your world", finds items and documents.

#One item

Open any body in the sky, or any row on home, and its drawer opens in place: when it is due, what section and type it is, how often it comes round, what it costs, who provides it, its reference and its reminders, then your notes and the documents attached to it, stored encrypted. Press a document and a preview stands beside the drawer; press the preview to read the whole thing. From the drawer you can snooze it, complete it, attach a document or retire it; the pencil edits it in place, picking dates from a calendar. Complete it and Orbit works out the next date for you.

#The inbox

Everyone gets their own relay address. Forward a bill or a policy to it and the inbox shows "what your relay has caught": what Orbit read from the attachment, and whether the attachment passed the malware scan. Nothing is added until you choose "Add to orbit". Anything left unreviewed is removed after 45 days, and Orbit only ever reads copies of your mail. An administrator sets up the mailbox first: see the mailbox.

#Settings

Settings holds your own choices: how you sign in, which of the five themes your sky uses (star-chart, after dark, clouds, dawn and retrograde; after dark is the default), when reminders arrive and whether by email or browser alert, and your relay address. "Watch the tour" replays the short tour film that Orbit offers once you have a household. Settings for the whole instance live on the administration screen instead.

sections.title: Around your household
sections.html:
#Around your household

  • Share the load. A household's owner can add people who already have an Orbit account, or send an invitation by email. Owners can also hand the household over to someone else.
  • Sections that fit. Home, Vehicles, Devices and Services to begin with. Add, rename, reorder and recolour your own.
  • On your phone. The main screens have their own phone layout. Orbit installs like an app and can send browser alerts. Your household's data stays on your server: the app keeps no copy of it on the phone, and changes are never saved up to send later.
  • Private by design. Use Orbit's own accounts, or an identity provider you already run (any OpenID Connect provider, such as Authentik). Nobody sees a household without signing in. See Authentication.

sections.title: One app. Standard parts.
sections.html:
#One app. Standard parts.

  • You bring a Linux machine with Docker, and an HTTPS address for it.
  • It runs three containers: Orbit itself, the official PostgreSQL 18 image for your records, and the official ClamAV image, which checks every upload before it is kept. ClamAV wants about 4 GiB of memory. An administrator can turn scanning off, and Orbit then marks later uploads as not scanned.
  • If you like, add email reminders, browser alerts, an identity provider and the mailbox your relay forwards into. Two heavier services are also optional: a document text reader (Apache Tika) and a private AI model server (Ollama). See Running Orbit.
  • Your data stays on your own disk: records in the database, documents encrypted with a separate key for each one. Encryption at rest says what that protects and what it does not.
  • Updates: run the launcher again and choose Update. Every release is pinned to one exact build, and your settings carry over. See Installing Orbit.
